title: Async & the Event Loop
tagline: How JavaScript handles thousands of operations on a single thread

sections.content:
JavaScript is single-threaded. At any moment, only one piece of JavaScript code is running. And yet Node.js servers handle tens of thousands of concurrent HTTP requests. Browser UIs stay smooth while fetching data from five different APIs. A single-page app streams real-time stock prices without freezing the scroll bar. How is any of this possible?

The answer is the **event loop** — a deceptively simple scheduling mechanism baked into every JavaScript runtime. Understanding it precisely means you can predict *exactly when* your code runs, *why* some callbacks fire before others, and *how* to structure asynchronous work so it stays readable, correct, and performant.

This topic builds the full picture in layers. We start with the physical problem: I/O operations take thousands of times longer than CPU operations, so you cannot just wait for them. We trace how the runtime deals with that reality — the call stack, the Web API sandbox, the task queues — and show exactly what the event loop does on every tick. We then walk through the three generations of async syntax: raw **callbacks**, **Promises**, and **async/await**, explaining not just how to write each but what each one compiles down to at the event loop level. Finally we cover the tricky edge cases — microtask starvation, unhandled rejections, the Node.js libuv phase model — that separate engineers who merely use async from engineers who understand it.

A word on terminology before we dive in: JavaScript the *language* has no event loop — that is a runtime concept. The event loop lives in **V8 + libuv** (Node.js) or in **V8 + the browser host** (Chrome). The language specification does define Promises and microtask ordering, but the plumbing that calls your code belongs to the embedding environment.

sections.title: The Single Gate Agent at a Busy Airport
sections.content:
Picture a single **gate agent** (the JavaScript call stack) processing passengers (tasks) at a boarding gate. The critical rule: only one passenger at the counter at a time — no parallel service, no exceptions.

When a passenger needs a boarding pass reprinted, the gate agent hands the request to the **printer room** (Web APIs / libuv) and immediately starts serving the next passenger in line. The gate agent does not stand idle waiting for the printer. While the agent processes passengers, the printer finishes its work and places a slip in one of two trays: an **urgent tray** (the microtask queue, for Promise callbacks) or a **regular tray** (the macrotask queue, for setTimeout callbacks and I/O events).

The gate agent's protocol — the event loop — has a strict rule: after each passenger, check the **urgent tray first** and process every slip in it, including any new slips that land there during processing, before reaching into the regular tray for the next passenger. This is why `Promise.then` callbacks always run before `setTimeout` callbacks scheduled at the same logical moment: the urgent tray (microtask queue) is always drained completely before the next regular passenger (macrotask).

The printer room corresponds to native code running in separate OS threads — it can do real parallel work. But the gate agent itself, the part that runs your JavaScript, is always a single person, never cloned.

sections.title: The Call Stack: How Synchronous Execution Works
The Web APIs Sandbox: Where Async Work Actually Happens
sections.content:
When you call `setTimeout`, `fetch`, `fs.readFile`, or `addEventListener`, you are not scheduling work inside JavaScript. You are handing a request to the **host environment** — the browser's Web API layer or Node.js's libuv — and immediately returning. The host environment processes the request using native code, often in a separate OS thread or via kernel async I/O (epoll, kqueue, IOCP).

**Browsers** expose Web APIs as C++ implementations inside the browser engine: `XMLHttpRequest`, `fetch`, `setTimeout`, `requestAnimationFrame`, `WebSockets`, `IndexedDB`, `Geolocation`. These live outside V8 itself.

**Node.js uses libuv**, a C library that provides:
- A **thread pool** (default 4 threads, configurable via `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`) for file system operations, DNS lookups, and crypto — operations that have no non-blocking OS primitive on all platforms.
- **Kernel-level async I/O** (`epoll` on Linux, `kqueue` on macOS, IOCP on Windows) for network sockets and pipes — these truly non-blocking operations do not need threads.

The critical insight: **libuv threads are not JavaScript threads**. They run native C code. When they finish, they enqueue a completion event for the JavaScript event loop to pick up and run the JS callback on the main thread. JavaScript itself always stays single-threaded. The parallelism is in the native layer, invisible to JS code.

This is why `fs.readFile` is non-blocking: the JS call returns instantly, libuv dispatches the read to a thread pool worker, your JavaScript continues running, and when the OS finishes the read, libuv posts the result callback to the macrotask queue.

sections.title: Microtasks vs Macrotasks: The Two Queues
sections.content:
The runtime maintains two distinct queues with different priorities. Getting their semantics wrong is the source of the majority of subtle async bugs.

**Macrotask queue** (also called the task queue or callback queue): holds callbacks scheduled by `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `setImmediate` (Node.js), I/O completion callbacks from libuv, and UI event handlers (click, keydown, etc.). The event loop takes **exactly one macrotask** per iteration, runs it to completion, then re-checks the queues.

**Microtask queue**: holds callbacks from `Promise.then`, `Promise.catch`, `Promise.finally`, `queueMicrotask()`, and `async/await` resumptions. After every task (synchronous chunk or macrotask), the runtime drains the **entire** microtask queue before doing anything else — including rendering the next frame in browsers.

The ordering rule per event loop tick:
1. Run the current synchronous code until the call stack is empty.
2. Drain the microtask queue: run every microtask, and if a microtask enqueues more microtasks, run those too — loop until the queue is completely empty.
3. (Browser only) If a render is due (typically every ~16 ms for 60 fps), update the DOM and paint.
4. Pick **one** macrotask from the macrotask queue and run it.
5. Go to step 2.

**Why this ordering matters:** Promise callbacks can starve the macrotask queue. If you write `while(true) { await Promise.resolve(); }`, you create an infinite stream of microtasks that never allows a macrotask — or browser rendering — to occur. The loop looks async (it uses `await`) but acts like a synchronous infinite loop for all practical purposes.

sections.title: Callbacks: The Original Async Pattern
Promises: Structured Async with Chainable Results
sections.content:
A **Promise** is an object that represents the eventual completion (or failure) of an asynchronous operation. It can be in one of exactly three states: `pending` (not yet settled), `fulfilled` (completed successfully with a value), or `rejected` (failed with a reason). Once settled — fulfilled or rejected — a Promise's state never changes. This immutability is fundamental: you can share a resolved Promise safely, attach `.then` handlers after the fact, and compose Promises without race conditions.

The Promise API:
- `new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... })` — construct a Promise; call `resolve(value)` or `reject(reason)` from inside.
- `.then(onFulfilled, onRejected)` — register handlers; returns a *new* Promise.
- `.catch(onRejected)` — shorthand for `.then(undefined, onRejected)`.
- `.finally(onFinally)` — runs regardless of outcome, passes value through unchanged.
- `Promise.resolve(value)` — returns an already-fulfilled Promise.
- `Promise.reject(reason)` — returns an already-rejected Promise.
- `Promise.all([p1, p2, ...])` — fulfills when all fulfill; rejects if any rejects.
- `Promise.allSettled([p1, p2, ...])` — waits for all to settle (fulfilled or rejected), never rejects.
- `Promise.race([p1, p2, ...])` — settles with the first settled Promise.
- `Promise.any([p1, p2, ...])` — fulfills with the first fulfilled; rejects only if all reject.

Chaining is the key feature that escapes callback hell:

```js
readFilePromise('config.json')
  .then(data => JSON.parse(data))
  .then(config => fetchUser(config.userId))
  .then(user => saveToCache(user))
  .catch(err => console.error('Pipeline failed:', err));
```

Each `.then` receives the resolved value of the previous Promise and returns a new Promise. A single `.catch` at the end catches any rejection anywhere in the chain. The flat structure is a dramatic improvement over nested callbacks.

Critically: **`.then` callbacks are always asynchronous**, even for already-resolved Promises. `Promise.resolve(42).then(v => console.log(v))` does not log 42 synchronously — the callback is scheduled as a microtask. This predictability is intentional and prevents Zalgo-style bugs (functions that sometimes call callbacks synchronously, sometimes asynchronously).

sections.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> pending
  pending --> fulfilled: "resolve(value)"
  pending --> rejected: "reject(reason)"
  fulfilled --> [*]
  rejected --> [*]
sections.caption: A Promise transitions from pending to either fulfilled or rejected — never back, never to both. Once settled, its value is immutable.

sections.title: async/await: Synchronous-Looking Async Code

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The parallel pattern with `Promise.all` is critical to understand. Sequential `await` calls serialize I/O operations needlessly. Starting both fetches before awaiting either gives true concurrency at the network level, dramatically reducing total latency when requests are independent. The sequential version takes T1 + T2 milliseconds; the parallel version takes max(T1, T2).

sections.title: The Node.js libuv Event Loop Phases
sections.content:
Node.js does not use the browser's event loop — it uses **libuv's phase-based event loop**, which is more complex. Understanding it matters for server-side JavaScript, particularly when mixing `setTimeout`, `setImmediate`, and I/O callbacks.

Libuv's event loop has six phases, executed in order:

1. **timers**: Executes callbacks from `setTimeout` and `setInterval` whose delay has elapsed.
2. **pending callbacks**: Executes I/O callbacks deferred from the previous iteration (e.g., some TCP errors).
3. **idle, prepare**: Internal libuv use only; not exposed to JS.
4. **poll**: Retrieves new I/O events and executes their callbacks. If the poll queue is empty and no timers are pending, it blocks here waiting for new I/O events. This is where Node.js spends most of its time at rest.
5. **check**: Executes `setImmediate` callbacks. This phase always runs after the poll phase — so `setImmediate` callbacks fire after I/O callbacks in the same iteration.
6. **close callbacks**: Runs callbacks for abruptly closed sockets and handles (e.g., `socket.on('close', ...)`.

After each phase transition, Node.js drains all **microtasks** (Promise callbacks and `process.nextTick` callbacks). `process.nextTick` is special: it runs before any I/O event callbacks, even before other microtasks in the same microtask drain — making it a higher-priority microtask.

**`setImmediate` vs `setTimeout(fn, 0)`**: When called from within an I/O callback, `setImmediate` always fires before `setTimeout(fn, 0)` because the check phase follows the poll phase in the same iteration, whereas timers are in the next iteration. Outside I/O callbacks, the order depends on system timing and is non-deterministic.

  B --> C["idle / prepare\ninternal"]

  D --> E["check\nsetImmediate"]

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The Node.js phase ordering is testable and deterministic when inside an I/O callback. process.nextTick is a source of confusion: despite its name, it does not defer to the 'next tick' in the libuv sense — it fires before Promise microtasks, within the current tick's microtask drain. The chunked processing pattern is a practical technique for CPU-bound work in async contexts.

sections.title: Error Handling in Async Code

sections.content: **Historical context:** The event loop concept predates JavaScript. Event-driven I/O was pioneered by systems like `select(2)` in Unix (1983) and later `epoll` (Linux 2002), `kqueue` (FreeBSD/macOS 2000), and IOCP (Windows). Node.js (2009) brought this model into the mainstream for server-side JavaScript via libuv. Promises were standardised in ES6 (2015) after years of competing implementations (jQuery Deferred, Q, Bluebird). `async/await` arrived in ES2017 — the same feature had appeared in C# in 2012, and Python 3.5 in 2015. The current specification for the microtask queue is maintained by WHATWG in the HTML Living Standard (not the ECMAScript spec), which is why browser and Node.js microtask semantics were historically inconsistent — they have since converged.

**Common mistakes and interview traps:**

**Mistake 1 — Sequential await for independent requests:** `const a = await fetch(urlA); const b = await fetch(urlB);` takes T_A + T_B milliseconds. Use `Promise.all([fetch(urlA), fetch(urlB)])` for T_max(A,B).

**Mistake 2 — Forgetting await:** `async function save() { db.save(data); }` — `db.save` returns a Promise that is never awaited. Errors are silently lost. Always await Promises or return them.

**Mistake 3 — await in a non-async callback:** `[1,2,3].forEach(async id => { await fetchUser(id); })` — `forEach` does not await the async callbacks; all three run concurrently and errors may be unhandled. Use `for...of` with `await` for sequential, or `Promise.all(items.map(...))` for parallel.

**Mistake 4 — Microtask starvation:** `while (running) { await Promise.resolve(); }` starves macrotasks. Yield with `setTimeout(r, 0)` every N iterations for CPU-bound loops.

**Interview insight:** When asked 'what is the event loop?', go beyond 'it handles async code'. Explain the call stack, the two queues, the microtask drain rule, and the single-thread constraint. That depth is what separates strong candidates.

items: The **event loop** enables non-blocking I/O on a single JavaScript thread: while the call stack is empty, it picks the next ready task from its queues and pushes it onto the stack.

**Microtasks** (`Promise.then`, `queueMicrotask`, `async/await` resumptions) run before **macrotasks** (`setTimeout`, I/O callbacks, `setImmediate`) — the entire microtask queue drains completely before one macrotask executes.
**async/await** is syntactic sugar over Promises with identical event loop semantics — each `await` is a microtask boundary where the function suspends and the event loop is free to run other work.
Blocking the call stack with synchronous CPU work (large loops, `readFileSync`) starves the event loop: no timers fire, no I/O callbacks run, no UI renders until the synchronous work finishes.

**libuv** (Node.js) handles I/O in a native thread pool and via kernel async primitives — JavaScript itself never blocks; only the native layer does real parallel work and posts results back to the JS queue.

The Node.js libuv loop has six phases; `setImmediate` fires in the check phase (after poll I/O) while `setTimeout(fn, 0)` fires in the timers phase of the next iteration — making `setImmediate` the reliable choice for post-I/O scheduling.

Unhandled Promise rejections crash Node.js 15+ by default — always attach `.catch()` handlers or use `try/catch` with `await`, and register a global `unhandledRejection` handler as a safety net in production servers.

quiz.question: In what order does the event loop process these, registered at the same moment: a `setTimeout(fn, 0)` callback (A) and a `Promise.resolve().then(fn)` callback (B)?
options: A then B — setTimeout was registered first
B then A — microtasks run before macrotasks
Simultaneously — the event loop runs them in parallel
A then B — setTimeout has higher queue priority
quiz.explanation: Promise.then callbacks are microtasks; setTimeout callbacks are macrotasks. The event loop drains the entire microtask queue before executing any macrotask, so B always runs before A regardless of registration order.

quiz.question: What is the output of: `console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C')); console.log('D');`?
options: A D C B
A B C D
A D B C
A C D B
quiz.explanation: Synchronous code runs first: A, then D. Then all microtasks drain: C (Promise.then). Then one macrotask: B (setTimeout 0). Final order: A D C B.

quiz.question: What does `await somePromise` do to the currently executing async function?
options: Creates a new OS thread to wait for the Promise
Blocks the entire JavaScript engine until the Promise resolves
Suspends the async function and schedules its continuation as a microtask when the Promise resolves
Converts the Promise to a synchronous value by polling
quiz.explanation: `await` suspends only the enclosing async function, returning control to the event loop. Other synchronous and async code can run. When the awaited Promise resolves, the continuation is scheduled as a microtask — not a new thread, not blocking.

quiz.question: Why does `fs.readFileSync('large.csv')` harm a production Node.js HTTP server?
options: It causes a memory leak in the V8 heap
It blocks the event loop thread, preventing all other requests from being handled during the read
Node.js does not support synchronous file reads at all
It creates too many OS threads in libuv
quiz.explanation: Synchronous I/O occupies the call stack for the entire read duration. Since Node.js has one event loop thread, no other requests, timers, or callbacks can run until readFileSync returns — every concurrent client stalls.

quiz.question: Which of these correctly runs two fetches in parallel and waits for both?
options: `const a = await fetch(u1); const b = await fetch(u2);`
`const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetch(u1), fetch(u2)]);`
`await fetch(u1); await fetch(u2);` inside a Promise.race
`setTimeout(() => fetch(u1), 0); setTimeout(() => fetch(u2), 0);`
quiz.explanation: `Promise.all` starts both fetches simultaneously and resolves when both complete, taking max(T1, T2) time. Sequential awaits take T1 + T2 time. The other options are incorrect or unrelated patterns.

quiz.question: In Node.js, libuv handles file system I/O using:
options: The JavaScript event loop thread via synchronous kernel calls
The V8 garbage collector's idle time
A native thread pool that posts completion events back to the JS event loop
A child Node.js process spawned per file operation
quiz.explanation: libuv maintains a native thread pool (default 4 workers) for file system operations. JS code is not involved during the I/O; when the OS finishes, libuv posts the completion callback to the macrotask queue for the JS event loop to execute.

quiz.question: What happens if microtask handlers continuously enqueue more microtasks?
options: A RangeError is thrown after a fixed number of microtasks
The macrotask queue and browser rendering are blocked indefinitely — microtask starvation
Nothing unusual — microtasks enqueued inside microtasks run in the next tick
The event loop automatically promotes them to macrotasks after 1000 microtasks
quiz.explanation: The event loop drains ALL microtasks before any macrotask. If microtask handlers keep enqueuing new microtasks, the loop never advances — blocking timers, I/O callbacks, and browser rendering. This is called microtask starvation.

quiz.question: In Node.js, when called from inside an I/O callback, which fires first: `setImmediate` or `setTimeout(fn, 0)`?
options: setTimeout(fn, 0) — it was designed as the earliest possible deferral
setImmediate — it runs in the check phase immediately after the poll phase in the same iteration
They are equivalent and fire in registration order
Neither — both wait until all microtasks drain
quiz.explanation: Inside an I/O callback, the libuv event loop is in the poll phase. After poll completes, it enters the check phase where setImmediate callbacks run — before returning to the timers phase for setTimeout callbacks. This ordering is deterministic inside I/O callbacks.

quiz.question: What is wrong with: `[1, 2, 3].forEach(async id => { const user = await fetchUser(id); await saveUser(user); })`?
options: async/await cannot be used inside forEach callbacks
forEach does not await the async callbacks — all three run concurrently without error propagation to the outer scope
fetchUser and saveUser must be called without await inside forEach
The code is correct and processes users sequentially
quiz.explanation: forEach calls each callback and immediately moves to the next regardless of the returned Promise. All three async callbacks start concurrently. Errors are unhandled Promises — they won't propagate. Use `for...of` with `await` for sequential, or `Promise.all(items.map(...))` for parallel with proper error handling.

quiz.question: In Node.js, what is the relationship between `process.nextTick` and `Promise.resolve().then`?
options: They are identical — both are microtasks with the same priority
Promise.then fires before process.nextTick because Promises have higher spec priority
process.nextTick fires before Promise.then — it has its own higher-priority queue drained first
process.nextTick is a macrotask; Promise.then is a microtask
quiz.explanation: Node.js processes the nextTick queue before the Promise microtask queue in each microtask drain cycle. Both are 'microtask-like' but process.nextTick has higher priority. This is Node.js-specific behaviour; browsers have no equivalent to process.nextTick.
